title: Barolo
subtitle: The king of wines
objectives: Explain the MGA system and the Barolo wars

steps.title: Eleven villages
steps.body: Barolo DOCG covers 11 villages south-west of Alba. Two soil types matter: Tortonian marl, in the west around La Morra and Barolo, gives more perfumed, softer wines; Serravallian sandstone and marl, in the east around Serralunga and Monforte, gives more powerful, tannic wines. Barolo must be 100% Nebbiolo.

steps.title: Ageing and vineyards
steps.body: Barolo must age at least 38 months, 18 in wood; Riserva 62 months. Since 2010, labels can name 181 MGAs, Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, the officially defined vineyard areas, like Cannubi, Brunate and Monprivato. They work like Burgundy's crus.

steps.prompt: Which part of Barolo gives the most powerful, tannic wines?
options: Serralunga and Monforte, in the east
steps.explanation: Serravallian soils in the east give more structure.

steps.title: The Barolo wars
steps.body: From the 1980s, modernists, like Elio Altare, used short maceration and new French barriques for softer, fruitier Barolo. Traditionalists, like Bartolo Mascarello, kept long maceration and large old Slavonian casks, called botti. The debate split the region. Today many producers blend both approaches.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Barolo's 11 villages split into Tortonian and Serravallian soils
It ages at least 38 months; labels can name 181 MGAs
The Barolo wars pitted barriques against botti
